transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-03-30
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Jamie Liu (Redwood AE), Nina Patel (Redwood SE), Omar Reyes (Redwood Infra SE), Marcus Reed (Cascade AI CTO), Priya Sharma (Cascade AI ML Eng), Liam O'Neill (Cascade AI Infra), Sara Gomez (Cascade AI PM)

Auto-summary (auto-generated):
Call is a deep dive into prefix caching strategies. Customer is evaluating Redwood for low-latency chat and long-context assistants. Concern areas include hit rate assumptions for short vs long prefixes, how cache keys should be constructed to avoid PII/bias, multi-tenant safety, and behavior when falling back to quantized models on Dedicated or Private clusters.

---

[00:00] Jamie Liu: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick audio check, you can hear me?
[00:04] Marcus Reed: Yep, loud and clear.
[00:06] Nina Patel: Good to go. I'm Nina from Redwood, I'll drive the technical part today.

[00:20] Jamie Liu: We scheduled 60 mins to go deep on prefix caching — hit rates, key design, and the implications for multi-tenant safety and VPC/on-prem. Marcus, can you give a 2-minute rundown of your use case?
[00:33] Marcus Reed: Sure. We're building a customer support assistant with long-context histories — agents plus prior messages plus docs. Main thing is we want sub-200ms generation latency for first token in interactive flows, and we expect long tails of context up to 12k tokens. We think a lot of cost can be saved if common prefixes (system prompts + recent turns) are cached. But we need to be careful about PII and tenant separation.

[01:05] Priya Sharma: Also we use a mix of deterministic prompts and dynamic user history, and we saw in earlier tests that naive keying gives very low hit rates because user tokens change slightly.

[01:18] Nina Patel: Right. So we'll walk through three parts: 1) what we mean by prefix cache vs KV cache, 2) cache key patterns and hygiene, and 3) performance characteristics — hit rate modeling and batching interactions.

[01:35] Nina Patel: Quick definitions: prefix cache is essentially caching the transformer activations for a prefix sequence so generation resumes from cached KV state; KV cache often refers to the runtime-managed key/value cache for attention during autoregression. In Redwood we expose prefix caching on the serving layer as an optional layer that stores serialized KV states per prefix key. That gets reloaded on subsequent requests to avoid recomputing the forward pass for the prefix.

[02:12] Liam O'Neill: Question — is the prefix cache per-model-version?
[02:16] Nina Patel: Yes, cache entries are tied to model id + model version + quantization/profile flags + tokenizer version. If any of those change we invalidate the entry.

[02:30] Marcus Reed: Good. We do model rollouts frequently — how do we avoid staleness during canary?
[02:35] Omar Reyes: We recommend using a versioned key namespace. For canary you can optionally route a small percentage of traffic to new keys, and Redwood supports TTL-based eviction plus manual invalidation APIs. We also support cross-model compatibility if you provide mapping, but by default different model ids mean different caches.

[03:05] Priya Sharma: Let's talk about cache keys. We looked at your docs but need concrete patterns — what do teams use in practice?
[03:12] Nina Patel: Common pattern: deterministic canonicalization of the prefix + hashed metadata. E.g., compute canonical_prompt = canonicalize(system_prompt + few_shot + last_N_user_turns) then key = sha256(model_id + tokenizer_version + quant_flags + canonical_prompt_hash + tenant_id(optional)). We push hashing to avoid storing raw PII in the cache key.

[03:46] Sara Gomez: When you say canonicalize, do you strip timestamps and session ids?
[03:50] Nina Patel: Yes — strip volatile bits, normalize whitespace, optionally redact or encode user-specific tokens. This increases hit rates for shared prompts. But there's a tradeoff: over-normalizing can leak personalization — so for multi-tenant setups include tenant_id in the key namespace.

[04:12] Marcus Reed: For our use case, system prompt and product-specific docs are the common prefix. The user history is the variable part. Should we only cache system+docs and compute user history on the fly?

[04:24] Nina Patel: That's a very common approach. Cache the static prefix (system + docs + few-shot examples) and then append dynamic turns. Redwood supports hierarchical caching — we can store multiple prefix segments. On request, we can compose cached KV states: e.g., load cached state for static_prefix then run forward pass for last_k user tokens — smaller compute. That often yields very high effective hit rates for static content.

[04:55] Priya Sharma: Are there limits on how many prefix segments you can compose?

[04:58] Omar Reyes: There's an operational overhead but we commonly see up to 3-4 segments composed without noticeable penalty. Compose cost is essentially a small linear pass to merge KV caches and it avoids re-encoding repeated static docs.

[05:20] Nina Patel: Hit rate modeling: We usually recommend measuring two things — absolute hit rate for exact keys and effective hit rate for hierarchical composition. For example, if static prefix covers 70% of tokens and dynamic tail is short, you can get >60% compute reduction even with low exact-key hits.

[05:43] Marcus Reed: Can you share realistic hit-rate numbers? We told execs '50% cost savings' and want to sanity check.

[05:48] Nina Patel: In our benchmark with customers of similar patterns, caching static system+doc prefixes often yields 40-70% token compute savings. If you canonicalize prompts aggressively and tenants share many common prompts, you can reach 70%+. But for personalized chat logs where almost every message differs, you might only get 10-25% without hierarchical segmentation. So your dataset profile matters.

[06:20] Priya Sharma: Important: what about tenant safety — can cache entries leak across tenants?

[06:25] Nina Patel: Redwood enforces namespace isolation by default for multi-tenant accounts. Cache entries include tenant_id somewhere in the key by default for hosted/dedicated. For Private deployments you can choose per-tenant namespaces or a global store depending on your needs. We don't recommend global caches unless you are deliberately sharing non-sensitive templates.

[06:45] Liam O'Neill: For Private on-prem, our security team is strict — we need cache stored on customer side only and encrypted at rest.

[06:50] Omar Reyes: That's supported. For Private we can keep cache storage in a customer-controlled bucket or mount encrypted NFS; entries are encrypted with your KMS. We log access and provide audit trails. We'll share the security appendix.

[07:10] Marcus Reed: Ok, what about interactions with KV cache and batching? Sometimes batching groups requests with different prefixes and that hurts latency.

[07:18] Nina Patel: Good point. Redwood's runtime does workload-aware batching: we prioritize matching prefixes for low-latency path, and we also allow per-route SLOs. If you set a tight latency SLO we will batch less aggressively for first-token latencies. There's an optimization where we pre-warm KV caches for common prefixes so the request hits hot cache and goes into a faster path.

[07:48] Priya Sharma: How does pre-warming work?

[07:50] Nina Patel: You can seed the cache via API with serialized KV states for known prefixes. Redwood also supports background TTL-based warmers that watch traffic patterns and precompute likely prefixes. For calls with seasonal workloads you can schedule pre-warm jobs.

[08:12] Marcus Reed: If we seed with a lot of prefixes, does that increase memory pressure?

[08:16] Omar Reyes: Yes, memory and storage usage scales with cached state size. Serialized KV state for 8k context can be tens of MBs depending on model and quantization. We provide size estimation tooling and recommend TTLs and LRU policies; Dedicated customers can set eviction thresholds per pool.

[08:40] Priya Sharma: Let's touch quantization: we sometimes run 4-bit quantized variants for cost. Are cached KV states interchangeable between quantized and non-quantized models?

[08:51] Nina Patel: No — KV states are tightly coupled to the numerical representation and kernel implementations. We include quant_flags in the cache key so a 4-bit model has separate entries. You can migrate by warming the new model's cache or by running a small conversion job that recomputes the KV state under the new precision.

[09:12] Jamie Liu: In cases where a quantized fallback is used for cost, we often recommend a short warm-up sample set to populate critical prefixes. That avoids first-request latency cliff.

[09:25] Sara Gomez: For A/B testing different model sizes, do you recommend separate cache namespaces?

[09:30] Nina Patel: Yes — treat model id as part of the key namespace. If you need cross-model reuse, you must provide canonical mapping and accept approximation risk.

[09:42] Marcus Reed: Let's talk about cold-start behavior. If a user hits a prefix not in cache, what is the impact on p95 first-token latency?

[09:50] Nina Patel: Cold start equals full forward pass for the prefix + decode. For very long prefixes that can add tens to hundreds of ms depending on model/GPUs. In our tests, recomputing a 4k-token prefix on A100-style hardware added ~120-220ms p95 compared to hot path. Using pre-warm or hierarchical caching typically keeps p95 bounds tighter.

[10:14] Priya Sharma: Any guidance on TTLs?

[10:17] Omar Reyes: TTLs depend on traffic patterns. For static docs you can set long TTLs (days-weeks). For dynamic content consider session-based TTLs (minutes-hours). Also set a max byte size per tenant to avoid runaway cache growth.

[10:34] Nina Patel: A security note: keys should not contain raw PII. Use hashing. If you need to tie to a user, consider tenant-scoped keys and store any minimal mapping in a separate encrypted index.

[10:50] Marcus Reed: How about logging and audit? We need to show auditors that cache reads are only for allowed tenants.

[10:56] Omar Reyes: We emit cache read/write logs with tenant_id, key_hash, model_id, and timestamps. For Private deployments logs can be shipped to your SIEM. We can also provide attestation reports for audit windows.

[11:15] Priya Sharma: Edge case — what if canonicalization causes collisions (different prompts map to same canonical form)? That's risky.

[11:22] Nina Patel: Collisions are possible if canonicalization is too aggressive. To mitigate, include a short non-reversible fingerprint of original (e.g., salted hash) and monitor warnings. We also support a sampling mode where we log both original and canonical forms (encrypted) to validate collisions before enabling aggressive normalization in prod.

[11:45] Liam O'Neill: From infra perspective, what are recommended hardware targets?

[11:50] Omar Reyes: For very low-latency interactive workloads we recommend GPUs with fast NVLink and high memory — A100 or H100 class. For Private clusters, pick nodes with >80GB vRAM for long contexts or use quantized models with sibling caching policies. Redwood's Dedicated offering can be sized with reserved pools optimized for prefix cache workloads.

[12:12] Marcus Reed: Anything else about multi-tenant safety?

[12:15] Nina Patel: One more: enforce RBAC on cache management APIs. Only system roles should invoke manual invalidation or seed operations. Also use tenant-scoped encryption keys if tenants require crypto separation.

[12:30] Sara Gomez: Ok let's talk practical pilot: what should we run?

[12:33] Jamie Liu: We propose a 2-week pilot: 1) collect representative prompt distribution from you, 2) seed static prefixes (docs + system prompts) and run comparative benchmarks (hot vs cached) for p50/p95 and token cost, 3) iterate keying pattern. We'll provide scripts and a dashboard.

[12:50] Marcus Reed: That sounds good. Priya, Liam — are you ok with providing sample traffic?

[12:55] Priya Sharma: Yes. We'll sanitize and sample. Expect to send by Apr 3.

[13:02] Liam O'Neill: Need to confirm VPC peering and private bucket options. Omar, Nina, can you follow up with exact network requirements?

[13:10] Omar Reyes: Yes, we'll share the VPC peering checklist and firewall stanza. Also include storage options for cache (S3 with KMS or NFS).

[13:20] Nina Patel: Quick Q&A — Marcus: any other concerns?

[13:22] Marcus Reed: Mostly audit and predictable p95. Also want to avoid unexpected cost regressions if caching rules are misapplied.

[13:29] Nina Patel: We'll add monitoring and regressions alerts into Redwood Optimize so if a cache hit rate drops or latency spikes you get notifications and automatic fallback to safe configs.

[13:38] Sara Gomez: Do you have a demo or sample config we can look at?

[13:41] Jamie Liu: We'll send the prefix-caching best-practices doc and a sample compose-config + benchmark script. Link we'll add in follow-up: https://redwood.example.com/prefix-caching-guide (redacted in call)

[13:55] Priya Sharma: One last thing — can caching work with streaming responses and tool-calls?

[14:00] Nina Patel: Streaming yes — once KV state is loaded we stream tokens normally. For tool-calls we mark tool insertion points as boundaries and treat tool responses as dynamic tails, the static system+docs prefix can still be cached.

[14:12] Marcus Reed: Great. Let's summarize next steps.

[14:15] Jamie Liu: Recap: Redwood to send docs, pre-warm scripts, VPC checklist, pricing for Dedicated pilot. Cascade to send sampled prompts and confirm pilot cohort/traffic. Set follow-up for pilot kickoff week of Apr 6. Action items captured in the meeting notes.

[14:35] Marcus Reed: Thanks everyone. This was helpful.

[14:37] Nina Patel: Thanks, we'll follow up.
